analysis.one_liner: Limits House campaign spending and bans soft money, bundled contributions, and most lobbyist donations.
analysis.headline: The Federal Election Reform Act of 1996 was referred to five House committees and never received a vote, dying at the end of the 104th Congress with only one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let House candidates who agreed to a $600,000 spending cap get half-price TV and radio ads and discounted campaign mail, while banning unlimited "soft money" contributions to national party committees, capping independent attack spending at $30,000 per House race, barring lobbyists who had recently contacted a member from contributing to that member, and banning leadership PACs run by officeholders. It was introduced in February 1996 and sent to five committees; no committee ever acted on it and it died when the Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, and House challengers and incumbents who lack access to big donors. Candidates who accept a $600,000 spending limit would get broadcast ads at 50 percent off the lowest rate, postage at nonprofit rates, and taxpayer-backed payments from a new Independent Expenditure Response Fund if outside groups attack them. The soft money ban, bundling ban, and limits on PAC and lobbyist money would reduce the influence of large corporate, union, and interest-group checks over who gets elected. Rules requiring 75 percent of individual contributions to come from the candidate's home state would shift campaigns toward constituents rather than national donors. A separate allowance with an even-year mass mailing ban would curb incumbents' taxpayer-funded newsletters during election season.

how_it_helps.text: Caps total House campaign spending at $600,000 per election cycle (with modest adjustments) for candidates who opt into the system, and limits candidates' use of their own and family money to 5 percent of that cap, so seats would not go mainly to the biggest spenders or self-funders.

Rewards candidates who comply with discounted broadcast rates at 50 percent of the station's lowest charge, anti-preemption protections so their ads actually air, and postage at nonprofit rates — cutting the cost of reaching voters for candidates without deep-pocketed backers.

Bans national party committees from soliciting, receiving, or spending unlimited 'soft money' and requires party spending that might affect a federal election to come from fully disclosed, federally limited funds — closing the loophole parties used to absorb six- and seven-figure donations from corporations and unions.

Bars any registered lobbyist or foreign agent from contributing to (or soliciting contributions for) a member of Congress if they lobbied that officeholder in the preceding year, directly separating paid influence-peddling from campaign money.

Caps independent 'express advocacy' spending at $30,000 per House race and, if courts struck that down, requires the FEC to pay a compliant candidate from a publicly financed Independent Expenditure Response Fund equal to the attack spending against them — blunting last-minute special-interest ad barrages.

Abolishes 'leadership' PACs controlled by federal officeholders, bans conduit 'bundling' of contributions by organizations and paid agents, treats young children's campaign contributions as their parents', and requires 75 percent of a House candidate's individual contributions to come from in-state residents.

Replaces the old franked mass-mailing rules with a dedicated, capped allowance and prohibits mass mailings postmarked during even-numbered-year sessions — limiting incumbents' ability to use tax dollars for self-promotion right before elections, with the savings designated to fund candidates' reduced postage.

analysis.who_pays: Political action committees, corporate and union treasuries, lobbyists, and wealthy donors would lose the channels they use to influence House elections: soft money to party committees, bundled contributions, leadership PACs, unlimited independent attack ads, and access to members they fund. Broadcasters would have to sell airtime to complying candidates at half their lowest rate and could not preempt it, with license renewals conditioned on compliance. Party committees would lose soft-money fundraising. Taxpayers would bear the cost of the Independent Expenditure Response Fund checkoff and the revenue lost from below-cost broadcast and postage rates, and House members would lose part of their official mail allowance.

drawbacks.text: Its mandatory candidate spending limit and $30,000 cap on independent expenditures conflict with the Supreme Court's Buckley v. Valeo line of cases, which holds that campaign spending itself cannot be capped — only contributions can — and the bill itself anticipates this by mandating expedited Supreme Court review of its constitutionality; much of its core could have been struck down.

The bill subsidizes campaigns with public resources: half-price broadcast time imposed on stations, below-cost postage, and a taxpayer checkoff-funded Independent Expenditure Response Fund that pays compliant candidates to match outside attack spending — costs shifted to broadcasters and taxpayers.

It layers on heavy new compliance: a $500 registration fee on every political committee, 48-hour reporting duties, and potential random FEC audits, which fall hardest on small campaigns and volunteer-run committees.

The 75 percent in-state contribution requirement could disadvantage candidates from states where many residents work in neighboring districts or in Washington, and the definition of who counts as an independent spender was detailed enough to invite litigation over coordination.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — closing the soft money gap, cutting the PAC-lobbyist conduit to House members, and making it affordable for non-wealthy candidates to compete — went to the heart of why ordinary voters feel Congress answers to donors. But the design was legally vulnerable: its mandatory spending and independent-expenditure caps ran into decades of Supreme Court precedent, so even had it passed, courts might have struck its core. The taxpayer and broadcaster subsidies it relied on were a real cost, though a modest one next to the money it would have redirected. On balance a serious reform bill, weakened by constitutional overreach rather than by a bad purpose.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in five House committees and two subcommittees for the rest of the 104th Congress, and no committee or the full House ever voted on it.

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn Maloney introduced the bill on February 1, 1996, and it drew a single cosponsor, a fellow House Democrat.

The Speaker referred it to five committees at once — House Oversight (as lead), Commerce, Judiciary, Government Reform and Oversight, and Ways and Means — splitting it across jurisdictions, a common way to slow a bill.
On February 13, 1996, it was sent to the Postal Service and Telecommunications and Finance subcommittees; no further action of any kind was taken for the rest of the Congress.
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, with the bill still in committee, so it died without a hearing, a markup, a floor vote, or a Senate counterpart ever being reached in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress, PACs, lobbying firms, and the national party committees came out ahead: the soft money, leadership PAC, bundling, and lobbyist-contribution channels the bill would have closed stayed open, and broadcasters kept charging full rate for candidate ads. Voters got no relief from special-interest money in the 1996 and 1998 House elections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent members, PACs, lobbyists, party committees

for.name: Rep. Carolyn Maloney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Federal Election Reform Act of 1996 and sought committee consideration.

for.name: One House Democratic cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: House Oversight Committee leadership (Chair William Thomas)
against.role: Chair of the lead referring committee, 104th Congress
against.what_they_did: The lead committee referred the bill to its Postal Service subcommittee on February 13, 1996 and took no further action; no hearing or markup was ever held.

against.name: Speaker Newt Gingrich
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor and assigned it to five committees, a multi-committee referral that fragmented consideration; the House never debated or voted on it.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no partisan split is on the record; the only two members of either party to support it were House Democrats, in a chamber Republicans controlled after 1994.

industries.industry: Political action committees and corporate/union special interests
industries.note: The bill would cap aggregate PAC giving per House race at $200,000, bar leadership PACs run by officeholders, end conduit bundling, cap connected organizations' support at 20 percent of a committee's fundraising costs, and impose a $500 registration fee — shrinking PACs' ability to buy access to House members.

Registered lobbyists and foreign agents could no longer contribute to, or raise money for, any federal candidate whose office they had lobbied within the past year — severing the pay-to-play link between lobbying contracts and campaign checks.

Stations would have to sell prime candidate airtime to complying House candidates at half their lowest rate, could not preempt it, and would have license renewal conditioned on compliance — a direct cut to political advertising revenue in the industry's highest-priced season.

The soft money ban would stop national and congressional party committees from raising and spending unlimited, undisclosed contributions, forcing all federal-affecting spending into fully limited and reported funds.

industries.industry: Wealthy self-funding candidates and big individual donors
industries.note: Personal and family spending would be capped at 5 percent of the spending limit, contributions to House candidates cut to $500, and 75 percent of individual contributions required to come from the candidate's home state, reducing the weight of a few rich donors in House races.
